lessons.title: Working with Primitives: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, bigint
lessons.description: Explore every primitive data type in JavaScript — the building blocks that hold all your data before you get to objects and arrays.

sections.heading: What are primitives?
paragraphs: Primitives are the most basic data types in JavaScript. They are immutable — once you create one, you cannot change it. You can only create a new value and reassign the variable. There are seven primitive types in total.

sections.heading: The seven primitives
list: string — text, always wrapped in quotes: "hello", 'hello', or `hello`
undefined — a variable with no assigned value
symbol — a unique identifier (we will explore this in topic 7.2)

sections.heading: Strings
paragraphs: A string is a sequence of characters wrapped in quotes. JavaScript does not care which quote style you use — single, double, or backticks — as long as you are consistent. Strings can hold any text: names, sentences, even entire HTML pages.

sections.heading: Numbers
paragraphs: JavaScript has one number type that covers integers, decimals, positive, negative, and special values like Infinity and NaN (Not a Number). There is no separate type for whole numbers vs. decimals — they are all just number.

sections.heading: Booleans
paragraphs: A boolean is either true or false. They are the result of comparisons and the backbone of conditional logic. When you write age > 18, the result is a boolean.

sections.heading: null and undefined
paragraphs: null means "intentionally empty" — you set it deliberately. undefined means "not yet assigned" — JavaScript gives this automatically when a variable has no value. They look similar but serve different purposes.

codeExamples.heading: Creating each primitive type
codeExamples.code:
let name = "Vishnu";           // string
let age = 25;                   // number
let score = 98.5;               // number (decimal)
let isLoggedIn = true;          // boolean
let nothing = null;             // null
let mystery;                    // undefined
let big = 9007199254740991n;    // bigint

console.log(typeof name);      // "string"
console.log(typeof age);       // "number"
console.log(typeof isLoggedIn);// "boolean"
console.log(typeof nothing);   // "object" (a known JS bug!)
console.log(typeof mystery);   // "undefined"
explanation: Each variable holds a different primitive type. Notice typeof null returns "object" — this is a long-standing bug in JavaScript, not something you did wrong.
A variable declared without a value (let mystery;) automatically gets undefined.
bigint uses the n suffix to distinguish it from regular numbers.

codeExamples.heading: String basics
explanation: All three quote styles create the exact same string. Use whichever you prefer — backticks are the most flexible because they also support template literals (covered in 1.4.4).
Strings have a .length property that tells you how many characters they contain.

practice.task: Create one variable for each of the seven primitive types. Use typeof on each and print the result.
hints: For undefined: just declare let x; without assigning a value.
practice.note: Notice that typeof null returns "object". This is a famous JavaScript quirk.

keyTakeaways: JavaScript has seven primitive types: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, and bigint.
Primitives are immutable — you create new values, you never mutate them.
Strings can use single, double, or backtick quotes — they all produce the same type.
typeof reveals a value's type, but watch out: typeof null returns "object" (a bug in JS).
lessons.challenge: Create a variable with a string, then try to change a single character in it (e.g. name[0] = "X"). What happens? Why?

lessons.title: Checking Types using the typeof Operator
lessons.description: Use the typeof operator to inspect what type of data a variable holds — and learn the one famous gotcha that catches everyone.

sections.heading: What is typeof?
paragraphs: typeof is a unary operator that returns a string describing the type of its operand. It works on variables, literals, and expressions. It is the primary way to check data types at runtime in JavaScript.

sections.heading: What typeof returns
list: "function" for functions (even though functions are technically objects)
"object" for objects, arrays, and null (the famous gotcha)

sections.heading: When typeof is useful
paragraphs: You will use typeof to validate user input, debug unexpected values, and write defensive code that handles different types gracefully. For example, before doing math on a value, you can check that it is actually a number.

codeExamples.heading: typeof with different values
codeExamples.code:
console.log(typeof "hello");     // "string"
console.log(typeof 42);          // "number"
console.log(typeof true);        // "boolean"
console.log(typeof undefined);   // "undefined"
console.log(typeof null);        // "object" (gotcha!)
console.log(typeof [1, 2, 3]);   // "object" (arrays are objects)
console.log(typeof {});          // "object"
console.log(typeof function(){});// "function"
explanation: Notice typeof null returns "object". This is a bug from the earliest days of JavaScript that was never fixed for backward compatibility. Remember it — you will be asked about it in interviews.
Arrays also return "object". To specifically check for arrays, use Array.isArray(value).
Functions are the only "object-like" value that typeof identifies correctly.

codeExamples.heading: Using typeof to validate input
explanation: This function checks the type before doing any math. If the input is not a number, it returns a helpful message instead of producing NaN.
This pattern — check first, act second — is called defensive programming and prevents many bugs.

practice.task: Write a function checkType(value) that prints "Number!" if the value is a number, "String!" if it is a string, and "Something else" for anything else. Test it with five different values.
hints: Use typeof value === "number" to check for numbers.
Chain with else if (typeof value === "string") for strings.
Use a final else for everything else.
practice.note: What does your function return for null? Remember the typeof gotcha.

keyTakeaways: typeof null returns "object" — this is a historical bug, not correct behavior.
Arrays return "object" too. Use Array.isArray() to check for arrays specifically.
Use typeof to write defensive code that validates input types before acting on them.
lessons.challenge: Write a function that accepts any value and returns a formatted string like: "Value: 42, Type: number". Test it with a string, number, boolean, null, undefined, and an array.

lessons.title: Using Numeric Separators for Readability (1_000_000)
lessons.description: Make large numbers easy to read by inserting underscores as visual separators — a small feature that makes a big difference.

sections.heading: Why numeric separators?
paragraphs: Large numbers are hard to read at a glance. Is 1000000 one million or ten million? Numeric separators let you insert underscores to group digits, making numbers as readable as 1_000_000. The underscores are purely visual — they do not affect the value.

sections.heading: The syntax
paragraphs: Place underscores between digits wherever it helps readability. Common patterns: every three digits for thousands (1_000), or every group of four for hex colors (0xFF_FF_FF). You can even use them in decimal numbers: 3.141_592_653.

sections.heading: Where they work
paragraphs: Numeric separators work in integer literals and decimal literals. They do not work inside strings — "1_000" is the string "1_000", not the number 1000. They also work with hex (0xFF_FF), binary (0b1000_0001), and octal (0o77_77) literals.

codeExamples.heading: Readable large numbers
explanation: The underscores make these numbers instantly readable. 7_900_000_000 is clearly 7.9 billion; 7900000000 takes effort to parse.
The runtime ignores the underscores entirely. 1_000 === 1000 is true because they are the exact same number.
You can place them anywhere between digits — there is no strict rule, just whatever helps you read.

codeExamples.heading: Hex and binary with separators
explanation: Hex colors become much clearer with separators: 0xFF_FF_FF is obviously white (255, 255, 255).
Binary masks group nicely in fours, matching the nibble structure of bytes.
Octal values also benefit from grouping.

practice.task: Rewrite these numbers using numeric separators: 100000, 5000000, 3.141592653589793, and 0xDEADBEEF. Verify each equals the original using ===.
practice.note: Try typing a number with two underscores in a row (1__000). What happens?

keyTakeaways: Numeric separators are underscores (_) placed between digits to improve readability.
They are purely visual — 1_000_000 is exactly the same value as 1000000.
They work in integers, decimals, hex, binary, and octal literals.
They do not work inside strings — "1_000" is a three-character string, not a number.
lessons.challenge: Create variables for these real-world values using numeric separators: the US national debt (~31 trillion), the distance from Earth to the Sun in km (~150 million), and the speed of light in m/s (~300 million). Print each.

lessons.title: Modern Template Literals (`Hello ${name}`)
lessons.description: Build strings dynamically using backtick syntax and embedded expressions — a cleaner alternative to string concatenation.

sections.heading: What are template literals?
paragraphs: Template literals are strings wrapped in backticks (`` ` ``) instead of single or double quotes. They let you embed variables and expressions directly inside the string using ${expression}. This replaces messy + concatenation with clean, readable syntax.

sections.heading: Embedding values
paragraphs: Inside backticks, anything between ${ and } is evaluated as a JavaScript expression. The result is converted to a string and inserted. You can put any expression inside: variables, math, function calls, even ternary operators.

sections.heading: Multi-line strings
paragraphs: Regular strings require \n for newlines. Template literals let you just press Enter — the string spans multiple lines exactly as you type it. This is especially useful for building HTML or long text blocks.

codeExamples.heading: Embedding variables in template literals
explanation: The ${name} syntax embeds the variable's value directly. No quotes around name — JavaScript evaluates the expression and inserts the result.
The old concatenation with + works but gets messy fast. Template literals are cleaner, especially with multiple variables.

codeExamples.heading: Expressions and multi-line strings
explanation: ${price * quantity} evaluates the math expression and inserts the result (147). Any valid JS expression works inside ${}.
The multi-line string spans multiple lines naturally — no \n needed. This makes building HTML templates much cleaner.
Notice the string includes a literal $ sign before the expression — it is not special, only ${ triggers evaluation.

practice.task: Create a template literal that says: "I am [name] and I am [age] years old. In 10 years I will be [age + 10]." Use your actual name and age. Print the result.
hints: For the math: ${age + 10} — expressions work inside ${}.
You can nest anything: functions, ternaries, even other template literals.
practice.note: Try building a small HTML snippet with a template literal. Notice how much cleaner it is than string concatenation.

keyTakeaways: Template literals use backticks (`) and ${expression} to embed values directly.
Any JavaScript expression works inside ${} — variables, math, function calls, ternaries.
Template literals span multiple lines naturally — no \n required.
They replace messy + concatenation with clean, readable syntax.
lessons.challenge: Build a receipt generator: create variables for item name, price, quantity, and tax rate. Use a template literal to print a formatted receipt with the subtotal, tax, and total. Example: "Coffee Qty: 2 × $4.50 = $9.00 Tax: $0.72 Total: $9.72"
